topic.readerProblem: Site owners need to know which AI crawlers exist, what each one does, whether to allow or block it, and what comparable sites actually do.
topic.connection: AI crawler access is the first technical gate for being retrieved and cited by ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and Google, which is the visibility AEOeye audits.

assessment: The page is the AI crawler directory plus AEOeye's October 2026 crawler access study (391 sites fetched, 384 with a usable robots.txt state). Every directory row is taken from the operator's own documentation fetched on 2026-10-03; study figures were recomputed from the published CSV and match the summary. It states a clear position (allow search and user-triggered bots, treat training bots as a business choice) and does not claim that any robots.txt setting changes whether an engine recommends a site.

artifacts.description: Per-site data for the 391 sites: robots.txt state, per-bot block and name flags, llms.txt, homepage fetch and JSON-LD results.
Study summary by segment with method, sample description and bot classification notes.
Dependency-free 24-case synthetic RFC 9309 robots.txt regression suite with expected output.
Dependency-free log analyzer separating claimed token, local category and optional operator-supplied CIDR verification.

methodology: On 2026-10-03 a self-identifying research crawler (AEOeyeResearch/1.0) fetched robots.txt, /llms.txt and the homepage of 391 sites chosen by AEOeye, once each, with a one-second gap per domain. robots.txt was parsed with the same matcher as AEOeye's SEO audit; a bot 'blocks' when its effective rules disallow the homepage. Denominators: 384 usable robots.txt states, 330 llms.txt checks, 312 parsed homepages.
limitations: Convenience sample skewed toward established brands, not a random sample of the web; one fetch per site on one day; main host only; robots.txt is a request and CDN-level blocking is invisible except when our crawler was challenged; the study measures access policy, not whether engines recommend a site.
